summaries.example: Think about a school concert. The chairs and people are objects. The singing, clapping, and leaving are events: things that happen. The concert has a beginning and an end, while a chair can stay in one place through the whole concert. We can describe the same event in different ways, such as “the band played” and “the music filled the room.” Philosophers ask whether these are one event or several events described differently.
summaries.summary: An event is something that happens or takes place. Smiling, walking, dancing, arriving, and thunder are examples. Philosophers compare events with objects, facts, properties, and times. Objects are things such as people and chairs; events happen to or are performed by them. A fact is what is true about something, while an event is the happening itself. A property is a feature, and time tells us when an event occurs. Some philosophers think events are real parts of the world. Others think ordinary sentences about events can be explained without adding events to what exists. There is also disagreement about whether different descriptions name one event or several. These questions matter because our language, seeing, planning, and explanations of causes all seem to involve happenings.
key_ideas: Events are happenings, while objects are things that take part in happenings.
A single event may have several descriptions. Philosophers disagree about when two descriptions pick out the same event.
Events can be connected with objects, facts, properties, and times, but they may not be identical to any of them.
Language often seems to talk about events. Words such as “walked,” “exploded,” and “slowly” can tell us what happened and how it happened.
summaries.why_it_matters: Thinking about events helps us understand stories, plans, causes, and everyday sentences. It also helps us notice that “what happened” is different from “what thing was there” and from “when it happened.” Asking careful questions about these differences is one way philosophers study how the world and our language fit together.

important_terms.definition: Something that happens, such as a walk, a clap, a storm, or a birthday party.
A thing, such as a chair, stone, or person, that exists and can take part in events.
A statement about what is true, such as the fact that the concert happened. A fact is not the happening itself.
A feature something can have, such as being red, loud, or heavy.
A stretch or point of time. Some philosophers explain events using the times when they happen.

questions_to_think_about: Is a person’s walk one event, or many smaller events such as steps?
Is “the ball broke the window” describing one event or two related events?
Can the same event be described as both helpful and noisy?
Would time still make sense if nothing ever happened?

summaries.example: Suppose a glass falls from a table, strikes the floor, and breaks. We might describe this as one falling-and-breaking episode, as a fall plus a collision plus a breaking, or as the glass’s failure to remain on the table causing damage. A theory of events must say what makes these descriptions refer to the same event or to different events. It must also explain how the event relates to the glass, the fact that it broke, the property of being fragile, and the interval during which it occurred.
summaries.summary: The entry examines what events are and how they differ from other metaphysical categories. Events include particular happenings such as actions, changes, processes, and perhaps static conditions. A familiar contrast says that objects exist and persist as continuants, whereas events occur and extend through time as occurrents. This contrast is contested: four-dimensional theories can treat objects and events as entities of one broad kind, while process theories may treat some processes as enduring continuants. Events are also distinguished from facts, which are abstract and not located in time in the same way. Further proposals identify events with property exemplifications, tropes, times under descriptions, or spatiotemporal regions under descriptions. The entry presents realist arguments from language, causation, perception, and action, alongside paraphrase-based antirealist strategies. It then considers event identity and essence: whether descriptions pick out one event or many, and which features an event could have had differently.
key_ideas: Events are commonly contrasted with objects by their modes of being: objects exist, whereas events occur, happen, or take place.

A standard distinction treats objects as continuants and events as occurrents, but some philosophers regard objects and events as varieties of four-dimensional entities, while others treat processes as continuants.
Events are usually distinguished from facts: a death occurs at a place and time, while the fact that someone died can be true in different places and times.
The status of events is disputed. Event talk may support realism through logical form, causal claims, and perceptual reports, but antirealist paraphrases attempt to avoid commitment to events.
Identity conditions are unsettled. The same happening may be described as a walk, a pleasant walk, or a particular bodily movement, and theories differ on whether these are identical.
The relation between events and times can be understood in either direction: events may be located in time, or times may be constructed from relations among events.
summaries.why_it_matters: The category of events connects metaphysics with semantics, cognitive science, and theories of action and causation. If events are genuine entities, they may help explain adverbial modification, causal relations, perception, and plural action. If event talk can be paraphrased away, philosophers must explain why that talk has its apparent logical structure. Disputes about event identity and essence also affect how we understand actions, mental causation, change, persistence, and counterfactual questions about what could have happened.

important_terms.definition: A particular happening, such as a specific walk or explosion, rather than a general kind of happening.
A repeatable kind or pattern of happening, such as rising or walking, of which particular happenings may be instances.
The metaphysical category of things that happen or occur, contrasted in the entry with objects, facts, properties, and times.
An entity that persists through time, such as an ordinary physical thing. Some theories treat objects as wholly present at each time they exist.
An entity that unfolds through time by having different temporal parts or stages. Events are often treated this way.
An abstract, generally timeless truth or state of affairs, such as the fact that a person died, contrasted with the death itself.
A repeatable feature or universal, such as redness or fragility. Some theories treat events as properties or property instances.
A condition that would have to hold for an entity to be the particular entity it is. The essential features of an event are debated.

questions_to_think_about: Does the sentence “Brutus stabbed Caesar with a knife” require an event in its logical structure, or can it be paraphrased without one?
If an action and a bodily movement occur together, what would make them one event rather than two?
Are an event’s participants, location, duration, and type essential to its identity, or can some vary?
Can a property such as “the sun’s rising” be an event, a repeatable event type, or a property of an interval?
If an omission is said to cause something, must the omission itself be a real negative event?

summaries.example: Imagine Maya walks to the library while listening to music. We can call this “Maya’s walk,” “Maya’s pleasant walk,” or “Maya’s trip to the library.” Are these three events, or three ways of describing one event? Now compare Maya with her backpack: Maya and the backpack are objects, but walking is an event. The walk takes time and has stages, while the backpack can remain the same backpack during the walk. Philosophers disagree about exactly how these categories fit together.
summaries.summary: Events are happenings: walks, storms, arrivals, decisions, explosions, and other things that occur. The entry compares them with objects, facts, properties, and times. Objects such as people and chairs are usually said to exist and persist, while events occur and unfold. Yet this familiar difference is debated. Some philosophers see both as extended through time; others think processes can endure more like objects. Events and facts are also distinct for many theories: a death happens at a particular time and place, but the fact that someone died is not located there in the same way. Other theories connect events closely with properties, times, or descriptions. The entry also discusses how verbs and adverbs seem to reveal an event structure in language. It asks whether events are needed in our picture of reality or whether our event-talk can be restated without them. Questions about one event’s identity and its possible features remain open.
key_ideas: Events are usually described as things that happen, while objects are things that exist and take part in what happens.
Philosophers disagree about whether objects and events are fundamentally different kinds of entities.
Facts are not normally the same as events: the event occurs at a particular time, while the fact can remain true regardless of where we discuss it.
Some theories treat events as individuals, some as properties or property instances, and some as times or regions together with descriptions.
Language gives reasons to take events seriously because adverbs, causal claims, and reports of seeing someone do something often seem to refer to events.
Events come in different forms, including activities, accomplishments, achievements, states, actions, and possibly events involving not doing something.
summaries.why_it_matters: Events are central to how we describe daily life. They help us talk about who did what, when something changed, why something happened, and how an action was performed. Understanding the debate can also clarify why the same happening may receive several descriptions. These ideas link philosophy to language, perception, planning, and explanations of causes without requiring that one philosophical answer be accepted.

important_terms.definition: Something that happens or takes place, such as a walk, explosion, arrival, or dance.
A thing that exists, such as a person, backpack, stone, or chair, and can participate in events.
Something true about the world, such as the fact that Maya walked. It is different from the walk itself.
A quality or feature, such as being pleasant, heavy, or red.
A particular happening, as opposed to a general kind of event that can happen again.
A happening that continues without a natural finish, such as walking for a while.
A happening aimed at a result, such as climbing a mountain or reaching a goal.
A relation in which an agent brings about an event or makes something happen.

questions_to_think_about: Is Maya’s walk the same event as Maya’s pleasant walk? Why might someone answer yes or no?
Can two events happen in the same place at the same time, or can only one event occupy a location?
Is resting a tree under static event, a state, or neither?
When someone raises an arm intentionally, is the action the same as the arm’s physical movement?
Does the sentence “The lights went out because nobody checked the switch” refer to a real omission or only describe what happened negatively?
